title: Nordholm Payments - Security review (data residency, audit logs, regional failover)
summary: Nordholm Payments reviewed Redwood Hosted controls for EU-only processing, audit logs, and failover behavior. Redwood confirmed planned/active region pinning controls (primary region + allowed region set) with deterministic enforcement at request time and blocked cross-region fallback by default. Customer requested documentation: residency policy/controls narrative, audit log event schema + samples, subprocessor region list, SOC 2 report, and retention details for logs/traces. Next steps: Redwood to send residency FAQ + internal policy excerpt, schedule a short technical follow-up on audit log export + SIEM integration, and confirm timeline for GA of hosted residency enforcement.
topics: EU-only data residency (Hosted API) and enforcement boundaries
Audit logging: admin config changes, access logs, export options
Regional failover / fallback: behavior when capacity constrained
Logging/tracing and whether prompts/completions can appear outside pinned region
Retention and deletion of request content, telemetry, and debug artifacts
SOC 2 / ISO narratives and evidence pointers
doc_requests: Data residency policy/controls doc for Hosted (what is guaranteed, what is excluded)
Audit log event schema + example payloads (policy create/update/delete, API key changes, admin overrides)
List of supported cloud regions for Hosted + internal region IDs (EU vs US breakdown)
Subprocessor list with processing locations (at least for Hosted telemetry/logging vendors)
SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certificate (if available) + security overview
Retention schedule for logs/traces and how to request deletion / configure retention where applicable
next_steps: Redwood (Avery) to email Nordholm: residency enforcement FAQ + overview of region pinning behavior (EU primary + allowed set) and failover rules.
Redwood (Marcus) to share audit log event list + a redacted sample export and confirm fields (actor, IP, timestamp, object IDs).
Nordholm to confirm which regions are acceptable for their policy (EU-only vs EU+UK vs EU+EEA) and whether any cross-region failover is ever allowed.
Schedule 30-min technical deep dive next week: audit log export to SIEM (Splunk) + requested retention controls.
Nordholm to send their internal requirement language for ‘deterministic residency enforcement’ and incident notification expectations.
transcript:
Meeting: Nordholm Payments - Security review (data residency, audit logs, regional failover)
Recorded: 2025-02-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Avery Johnson (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Marcus Lin (Security Eng)
Attendees (Customer): Lena Nordholm (VP Security), Tomas Berg (Security Architect), Priya Desai (Head of Compliance), Jonas Richter (Platform Eng)

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, thanks everybody for making time. This is Avery from Redwood. I’ve got Markus, our solutions engineer, and Marcus Lin from our security engineering team.

[00:10] Lena Nordholm: Hi. Lena here. Thanks. We’re trying to close the loop on a few items before we green-light the POC.

[00:17] Tomas Berg: Tomas, security architecture.

[00:19] Priya Desai: Priya, compliance.

[00:21] Jonas Richter: Jonas from platform engineering.

[00:24] Avery Johnson: Great. The agenda we sent was basically: data residency for Hosted, audit logs, and what happens when there’s regional failover or like capacity issues. We can also cover retention and what goes into logs.

[00:37] Lena Nordholm: Yep. And to be direct: we need EU-only processing for prompts and outputs. Not “best effort.” It’s like a hard requirement.

[00:46] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[00:47] Markus Klein: Yeah, makes sense.

[00:49] Marcus Lin: Yep.

[00:51] Tomas Berg: Also audit logging. We need to see who changed what, and we need to export to our SIEM.

[00:56] Avery Johnson: Cool. Markus, do you want to start with residency and then Marcus can cover audit events?

[01:01] Markus Klein: Sure. So on Hosted API today we already run in multiple regions. For enterprises like you, the plan we’re rolling out is region pinning at the org or project level, optionally at API key level. It’s basically: a primary region plus an allowed region set.

[01:18] Markus Klein: So for your case it would be something like primary=EU-West, allowed={EU-West, EU-Central} or something, depending what you accept.

[01:26] Priya Desai: And “EU-West” means where exactly? Like Ireland? Frankfurt? We need to be precise.

[01:32] Markus Klein: Yeah, sorry. The human labels map to cloud regions. We can share the exact region list; internally we map to region IDs. Typically EU-West is Ireland and EU-Central is Frankfurt, but we’ll confirm the exact mapping for Redwood.

[01:46] Tomas Berg: The big question is enforcement. Like, is it possible that if there’s an outage or just no GPUs, you route to US as a fallback?

[01:56] Markus Klein: By default with pinning enabled, cross-region fallback is blocked. So if the request can’t be served inside the allowed set, we return an error. We don’t silently move it to the US.

[02:07] Lena Nordholm: Okay. What error. Like a 500? Because we can’t debug that.

[02:11] Avery Johnson: Good call. We’re standardizing that.

[02:14] Markus Klein: The gateway returns a deterministic policy violation response. I think we’re landing on a 409, “conflict,” with a machine-readable error code. Marcus can confirm.

[02:24] Marcus Lin: Yeah. The contract we’re implementing is a consistent HTTP status, plus an error payload that includes an error_code like RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION, a request_id, and a help URL that points to docs.

[02:37] Tomas Berg: 409 is fine as long as it’s consistent across streaming. We saw vendors where streaming returns some generic 500.

[02:43] Markus Klein: Yeah, we’ve seen that too. Streaming is explicitly in scope. The first chunk of the stream, if it’s blocked, should be the same error envelope.

[02:52] Jonas Richter: On enforcement: what does “customer content” include. Prompts and completions obviously. What about embeddings inputs. What about tool calls. Like JSON schema.

[03:04] Marcus Lin: Our definition is basically: request payload that includes user-provided text, prompts, tool arguments if they include user content, model outputs. Anything that would be considered customer content is bound by residency in routing, background processing, and logs.

[03:19] Priya Desai: “Logs” is where things get fuzzy. We’ve had issues where debug logs include snippets.

[03:25] Marcus Lin: Yep. So we treat logs and traces as in-scope. The control is: we do not export prompt/response content across regions. We also restrict where logs are stored for that org. There is still metadata that can be cross-region, but it’s explicitly limited.

[03:42] Tomas Berg: What metadata.

[03:44] Marcus Lin: Typically things like request_id, timestamps, model identifier, latency numbers, token counts, and error codes. We avoid including the actual text content. And we can share the list of allowed fields.

[03:57] Lena Nordholm: So can you confirm: there is no scenario where the prompt leaves the EU region.

[04:04] Markus Klein: With pinning enforced and EU-only allowed set, we will not route the request to a US region. If we cannot serve in EU, we block. That’s the guarantee.

[04:16] Jonas Richter: What about like internal ops access. If your SREs are in the US, can they view the prompt from logs.

[04:23] Marcus Lin: Good question. We don’t log prompts by default. For rare cases where we enable deeper debugging, it’s gated and time-bound, and we treat it as customer content. For enterprise, we can put additional controls and approvals around any diagnostic capture.

[04:39] Priya Desai: Is that in writing somewhere? We need a doc that says what’s excluded. Like “support access” carve-outs.

[04:46] Avery Johnson: We have a residency policy and controls doc internally; we can share an enterprise-facing version plus the FAQ.

[04:54] Tomas Berg: Another edge case: Suppose the request enters in EU, but your control plane is in the US. Like the policy evaluation happens in the US.

[05:04] Markus Klein: The evaluation is done at the gateway / routing tier in-region. The policy is replicated as configuration, but the actual decision is at request time where the request is being handled. It doesn’t need to ship the payload to another region to decide.

[05:20] Jonas Richter: When you say replicated config, is that PII.

[05:23] Marcus Lin: Policy config is generally not customer content; it’s administrative data like allowed regions. That can be managed in the control plane. But we still audit any changes.

[05:35] Lena Nordholm: Okay. Let’s talk failover. If Frankfurt goes down, but Ireland is still up, we’re okay with that as long as both are EU.

[05:44] Markus Klein: Exactly. That’s the “allowed region set.” You can do EU-West and EU-Central. If EU-West is degraded, we can fail over within that set.

[05:55] Tomas Berg: But you said “block cross-region fallback by default.” Is there an option to allow cross-region fallback.

[06:02] Avery Johnson: We’ve heard some customers want it. For you, we’d recommend you keep it disabled.

[06:06] Markus Klein: There may be a config later that explicitly allows it, but it would be opt-in and very explicit, and you’d still have audit logs for the change.

[06:16] Priya Desai: From compliance: we cannot allow it. It would break our commitments.

[06:20] Avery Johnson: Yep, understood.

[06:23] Lena Nordholm: Now audit logs. We need: who changed residency policy, who created API keys, who changed RBAC, and any “admin override” events.

[06:35] Marcus Lin: That matches what we’re implementing. The audit log events include create/update/delete of residency policies, plus policy overrides or emergency bypasses (if any), API key lifecycle, and auth-related events. Each event includes: actor, actor type (user vs service), timestamp, IP, user agent if available, and the object affected.

[06:56] Tomas Berg: Are these logs in your console only, or can we export.

[07:00] Marcus Lin: Both. In-console view with filters, and export via API or an export sink. The export is basically JSON lines. We can also discuss S3 bucket delivery or webhook style.

[07:15] Jonas Richter: We’re Splunk. We can ingest from an S3-like bucket or HTTP event collector.

[07:20] Markus Klein: Got it.

[07:21] Avery Johnson: We can set that up as part of the POC if you want.

[07:25] Priya Desai: Retention. How long do you retain audit logs.

[07:29] Marcus Lin: Default retention depends on the plan; enterprise can extend it. Typical is 90 days in-product with export for longer. We should confirm exact numbers for your package.

[07:44] Priya Desai: And request logs. Like API access logs.

[07:48] Markus Klein: We have access logs and operational metrics. We don’t store the raw prompt by default. The access logs are mostly metadata.

[07:58] Tomas Berg: Okay, but I want to ask very specifically: do you store prompts or completions at rest for training.

[08:05] Avery Johnson: No.

[08:06] Marcus Lin: For enterprise, we do not use customer content for training. We can put that in the DPA / contract language. There are limited cases for troubleshooting with explicit opt-in.

[08:18] Lena Nordholm: We’ll need that in the security packet.

[08:21] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[08:22] Tomas Berg: Also sub-processors. Where are they. If you have some logging vendor in the US, that’s a problem even if you don’t send content.

[08:31] Marcus Lin: We maintain a subprocessor list with processing locations. For residency-pinned orgs, we ensure any systems receiving customer content are in-region. For metadata-only systems, there can be cross-region processing, but we can enumerate what that is.

[08:48] Priya Desai: This “metadata-only” thing—auditors will ask. They may still consider it data.

[08:54] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can provide the classification we use and the list of fields. Often that’s sufficient to show it’s not sensitive content.

[09:05] Jonas Richter: Can you talk about how routing works. Like, does the request hit a global load balancer and then get routed.

[09:12] Markus Klein: There is a global edge / gateway, but for pinned orgs we determine the region early and route directly to the in-region serving stack. The residency context is propagated downstream so no service accidentally goes “oh I’ll fallback to US because it’s cheaper.”

[09:28] Tomas Berg: So you’re passing like a header.

[09:30] Markus Klein: Essentially yes, a “decision context.” It’s not user-controlled; it’s internal.

[09:36] Lena Nordholm: If your EU region is saturated, you block. What’s the SLA story there.

[09:42] Avery Johnson: For Hosted, we can talk about an enterprise SLA with pinned capacity. If you need guarantees, Dedicated might be a better fit, but I know you prefer Hosted for speed.

[09:55] Jonas Richter: Dedicated would be ok if it’s still EU.

[09:58] Avery Johnson: Dedicated can be provisioned in specific regions as well, and it’s easier to ensure capacity. But you’d have more commitment.

[10:06] Lena Nordholm: For now we want Hosted but we might move to Dedicated if we hit issues.

[10:11] Markus Klein: That’s common.

[10:13] Priya Desai: We also need incident notification. If there is any residency breach, how fast are you telling us.

[10:20] Marcus Lin: We have incident response procedures and notification timelines in our enterprise terms. For a confirmed breach involving customer content, we notify per the contract. We can align the exact SLA in the MSA/DPA.

[10:36] Tomas Berg: We’ve seen incidents where a vendor says “best effort” and then later admits data went to US due to failover.

[10:43] Markus Klein: Yep, and that’s precisely why we’re making it a deterministic enforcement with block-by-default. It avoids silent movement.

[10:53] Lena Nordholm: Okay. Can you share the exact error codes you’ll use. We want our app to detect and alert.

[10:59] Avery Johnson: We can share that. It’s one of the docs.

[11:02] Marcus Lin: We have a small set: policy violation, invalid policy config, and “region not supported” kinds of things. We’ll send the list.

[11:14] Jonas Richter: For “invalid policy config,” what would that be.

[11:17] Markus Klein: Example: if a customer sets primary region to EU-West but allowed regions doesn’t include it, we reject. Or if they choose a region where a model isn’t available. The console will validate, but the API still enforces.

[11:35] Tomas Berg: Nice.

[11:36] Priya Desai: I want to talk about evidence: SOC2 Type II and ISO. Do you have both.

[11:41] Avery Johnson: SOC 2 Type II yes. ISO—let me confirm what we can share. We can definitely provide our security overview and the SOC report under NDA.

[11:51] Marcus Lin: And we can provide a control mapping narrative for residency enforcement when it’s GA.

[11:59] Lena Nordholm: Timeline. When is this pinning enforcement actually available. Is it now or future.

[12:06] Avery Johnson: It’s in flight. We can enable it for your POC in an allowlisted way, and then GA is planned shortly after.

[12:13] Markus Klein: Yeah, we have it behind feature flags in staging and rolling to production in phases. We can talk specifics offline.

[12:22] Tomas Berg: We’d prefer not to be the first customer.

[12:25] Avery Johnson: Totally fair.

[12:26] Marcus Lin: We already have multiple design reviews and internal testing on it. We can share what we can about validation and e2e tests.

[12:37] Jonas Richter: What about traces. You said traces are in-scope. Are you using like OpenTelemetry with a central collector.

[12:45] Markus Klein: We use tracing, yes. The key is that any spans that might include request attributes that are customer content are scrubbed. For pinned orgs, we keep trace storage in-region. There is still platform-level metrics that can be aggregated globally, but again without content.

[13:04] Tomas Berg: We’d like that written. We had a vendor that said “we scrub,” and then we found prompt fragments in trace attributes.

[13:12] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can provide the logging policy: what fields are allowed, what is redacted, and what’s blocked.

[13:20] Priya Desai: Also: who can change the policy. We need RBAC and ideally SSO.

[13:25] Avery Johnson: Enterprise console supports SSO/SAML and RBAC. You can restrict policy changes to admin roles.

[13:33] Lena Nordholm: Do you have MFA.

[13:35] Avery Johnson: Yes.

[13:36] Marcus Lin: And all those changes are audit logged.

[13:40] Tomas Berg: One more question: does region pinning apply to “background processing.” Like if you do caching or evals.

[13:47] Markus Klein: Caching is in-region. We don’t do cross-region content replication for Hosted as part of this. That’s actually a non-goal. So caches are local.

[13:59] Jonas Richter: Okay, so no multi-region replication.

[14:02] Markus Klein: Correct. It’s request routing and logging boundaries. Multi-region replication is a separate project.

[14:09] Lena Nordholm: That’s fine.

[14:11] Avery Johnson: Can I pause and check if we’re hitting the big questions.

[14:14] Lena Nordholm: We’re close. I need the docs and I need confidence that enforcement is real and auditable.

[14:22] Marcus Lin: On auditable: We’re emitting residency decision logs internally that record: which policy was evaluated, selected region, and if blocked, the reason. The customer will see blocked request counts and sample request IDs in the console, without content.

[14:40] Tomas Berg: Will we see “why” it was blocked.

[14:42] Markus Klein: You’ll see the reason class, like “attempted cross-region fallback” or “no capacity in allowed regions.” We won’t show internal capacity details, but enough to troubleshoot.

[14:56] Jonas Richter: That’s good.

[14:58] Priya Desai: Can you also confirm: your support team cannot just flip a bypass.

[15:04] Marcus Lin: If there is any bypass mechanism, it’s behind strict controls and audited. For enterprise, we can disable it or require customer approval. We can align on that in writing.

[15:17] Lena Nordholm: Great.

[15:18] Avery Johnson: Ok. Anything else on competitors or what you’re comparing against. Just so we know.

[15:23] Lena Nordholm: We looked at Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. They both have residency stories, but it’s complicated.

[15:29] Tomas Berg: And with OpenAI direct, it’s less clear. We need a clean story.

[15:35] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[15:37] Markus Klein: One thing: with our approach, the failure mode is explicit. Not silent failover.

[15:43] Tomas Berg: Yeah I like that.

[15:45] Avery Johnson: Okay, let’s talk about next steps and doc requests. Priya, can you list exactly what you need.

[15:52] Priya Desai: Sure. Residency policy doc—what is included, what excluded. Audit log schema and sample. Subprocessor list with locations. SOC2 report. And retention schedule for audit logs, access logs, and anything else.

[16:09] Avery Johnson: Great.

[16:10] Marcus Lin: We can also provide a short write-up on the enforcement boundary: routing, gateway, logging/tracing, and what metadata may be global.

[16:20] Tomas Berg: Also error codes list.

[16:22] Markus Klein: Yep.

[16:24] Avery Johnson: Perfect.

[16:26] (crosstalk)

[16:27] Jonas Richter: And just to be clear, for the POC we want EU-only. We can accept Ireland plus Frankfurt. Not UK.

[16:34] Markus Klein: Okay, EU-only, no UK. We’ll set allowed regions accordingly.

[16:39] Lena Nordholm: Great.

[16:41] Avery Johnson: Let’s schedule a technical follow-up. Markus, can you do next Tuesday same time.

[16:46] Markus Klein: Yeah.

[16:47] Avery Johnson: We’ll cover SIEM export integration and the console settings.

[16:52] Tomas Berg: Great.

[16:54] Avery Johnson: Anything else before we wrap.

[16:57] Priya Desai: Just: contract language. We will send our standard clause for data residency.

[17:03] Avery Johnson: Please do.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: And if you have language around incident notification timelines, send that too.

[17:10] Lena Nordholm: Okay.

[17:12] Avery Johnson: Awesome. We’ll follow up with the packet and the meeting invite.

[17:17] Lena Nordholm: Thanks.

[17:18] Tomas Berg: Thanks.

[17:19] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[17:20] Jonas Richter: Thanks.

(Transcript ends early due to Fireflies partial capture; remaining discussion was recap and scheduling per participants.)
